one_liner: Header-only SIMD/bswap array reversal for 1-16-byte elements; 8-16x faster than scalar libstdc++ std::reverse on bytes.
what_it_does: qReverse<ElementSize>(void* array, size_t count) reverses a contiguous array in place, treating each element as ElementSize raw bytes. Hand-written specializations exist for 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16-byte elements; any other size falls back to a plain swap loop with no speedup. It is not a drop-in std::reverse: it takes a pointer and an element count instead of iterators and is only valid for trivially copyable data.
how_it_is_fast: Instead of swapping one element pair per iteration, it loads a full vector from each end, reverses it in-register and stores it at the opposite end: pshufb (SSSE3), vpshufb plus a vperm2i128 lane swap (AVX2), vpshufb plus vpermq (AVX-512BW), vrev64q plus vext (NEON). The loops form a greedy cascade (widest vector first, then 64/32/16-bit bswap loops, then a scalar tail), and the ISA is chosen at compile time from predefined macros (__AVX512BW__, __AVX2__, __SSSE3__, __ARM_NEON) with no runtime dispatch. The scalar libstdc++ std::reverse it beats moves one byte pair per iteration and is bound by one store per cycle.
when_to_use: Reversing large contiguous byte buffers (roughly 1,000 to 1,000,000 uint8_t, e.g. flipping raw rows or byte strings) where your toolchain's std::reverse is still a scalar loop (GCC/libstdc++ in the measured setup; check your own compiler's output first).
Builds for a known ISA (-march=native, a fixed -mavx2 or AVX-512 fleet, ARM NEON boards) where compile-time ISA selection is acceptable.

2, 4 and 8-byte trivially copyable arrays (uint16_t, int32_t/float, uint64_t/double) only after measuring: the README tabulates 1-byte elements alone and a user report shows no gain or a loss at wider sizes.
As a worked teaching example of shuffle-based reversal: the README walks each ISA step with intrinsics and emitted assembly.
when_not_to_use: 16-byte elements on any AVX2 build: the AVX2 path scrambles element contents (see gotchas).

Current MSVC: microsoft/STL now ships a runtime-dispatched AVX2/SSE4.2 std::reverse for 1, 2, 4 and 8-byte trivially swappable types (__std_reverse_trivially_swappable_N in stl/src/vector_algorithms.cpp), so the VS2017 22.4x baseline is obsolete.

2/4/8-byte elements without your own benchmark: issue #2 (Clang 6, SSSE3, CPU not stated, 2019) measured 4,348 vs 3,911 ns at 10,000 uint16_t, 9,114 vs 3,962 ns for uint32_t and 18,955 vs 4,468 ns for uint64_t (qReverse vs std::reverse), closed by the reporter with no explanation.
Portable x86-64 binaries for unknown CPUs: without runtime dispatch you either compile with -mavx2 (illegal instruction on older CPUs) or get only the bswap path, since baseline x86-64 has no SSSE3.

Tiny arrays (8-32 bytes: 1.0-1.3x, within per-call timer overhead), non-trivially-copyable types, iterator-based generic code, or anything needing a maintained dependency (no commits since 2018-12-19).

integration.dependencies: none (standard headers plus x86intrin.h or arm_neon.h)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11); GCC or Clang with -mssse3/-mavx2/-mavx512bw or -march=native to enable the SIMD paths; MSVC support is fragile (see gotchas)
integration.platforms: x86/x86-64 (SSSE3, AVX2 and AVX-512F+BW paths, compile-time selected), 32/64-bit ARM with NEON, portable shift-and-mask fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the function keeps no state and writes only the caller's buffer, so concurrent calls on disjoint arrays are safe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — takes (void*, element count) plus the element size as a template argument instead of iterators, and is only valid for trivially copyable contiguous data

gotchas: Correctness bug (code reading, not executed): the qReverse<16> AVX2 loop calls _mm256_permute4x64_epi64(x, _MM_SHUFFLE(0,1,2,3)), which reverses all four 64-bit quadwords, so besides swapping the two 16-byte elements it also swaps the two 8-byte halves inside each element; the correct mask is _MM_SHUFFLE(1,0,3,2) (the AVX-512 path's _mm512_set_epi64(1,0,3,2,5,4,7,6) is right). tests/verify.cpp fills every byte of an element with the same value, so the half-swap is invisible and the Verify16 CTest cases pass. Every AVX2-enabled build corrupts 16-byte elements; the benchmarked 1-byte numbers are unaffected.

The per-ISA tables do not isolate the ISA: the i3-6100 'bswap' and 'AVX2' tables are nearly identical row by row (191 vs 189 ns at 10,000; 1,739 vs 1,714 at 100,000; 127 vs 127 at 6,133; 875 vs 875 at 50,432), the header compiles its AVX2 loop whenever -march=native defines __AVX2__, and 191 ns for 10,000 bytes is below the floor for 8-byte bswap stores at one store per cycle (about 338 ns at the i3-6100's fixed 3.7 GHz), while std::reverse's 2,740 ns matches one byte store per cycle (about 2,703 ns) (derived from page data). The 'bswap x15.8' column is most likely the AVX2 path, not a bswap-only result.

MSVC: the header's x86 branch tests __i386__/__x86_64__, which MSVC does not define, so MSVC builds fall through to the shift-and-mask Swap functions and include no intrinsics header (the SIMD paths then rely on intrinsics declared by some other include); MSVC does not traditionally define __SSSE3__, and CMakeLists.txt passes only /arch:AVX2, so reproducing the i9-7900X AVX-512 table needs /arch:AVX512 added by hand (its flags are not stated).

The bswap and scalar tail loops dereference the caller's buffer through uint16_t*/uint32_t*/uint64_t* at arbitrary byte offsets (misaligned, type-punned access, undefined behaviour in ISO C++): it works with GCC/Clang/MSVC on x86 and ARMv8, but UBSan's alignment check fires, and float or struct arrays reinterpreted as integers can in principle be reordered by type-based alias analysis when the call is inlined.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No sibling reverses arrays; vectorized_find, FastArrayOps and Leftpack are comparable single-purpose SIMD kernels for find, min/max and left-packing. Pick qReverse when std::reverse on byte (or, after measuring, 2/4/8-byte) buffers is a hot spot under GCC or Clang; on current MSVC the STL's own vectorized std::reverse covers the same ground.
verified_claims_summary: On an i3-6100 (Skylake, 3.7 GHz) built with g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native (GCC version unstated), qReverse<1> reversed in-cache byte arrays 8-16x faster than scalar libstdc++ std::reverse at 1,000-100,000 elements (2,740 vs 191 ns at 10,000) and 11.3x at 1,000,000, with no gain at 8-32 elements; an MSVC 2017 build on an i9-7900X peaked at 22.4x at 10,000 against the then-scalar MSVC STL. Each figure is the mean of 10,000 individually timed calls on the same zero-filled array, measured in October 2018 just before a performance-only fix to the later loops' block counters; only 1-byte elements are tabulated, and the bswap, SSSE3 and AVX2 columns probably do not each isolate one instruction set (see gotchas).
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-12-19 (last code change 2018-10-29) but MIT-licensed and a single ~900-line header that is easy to vendor; fix the 16-byte AVX2 shuffle mask and make tests/verify.cpp check bytes inside elements before relying on it, and on current MSVC prefer std::reverse.
